nameStory: Makino's stonecrop honors Japanese botanist Tomitaro Makino, who studied plants in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Like other stonecrops, it earned the 'stone' part of its name from its ability to thrive in rocky, seemingly impossible places where other plants would struggle to survive.
description: Makino's stonecrop is a small, low-growing succulent plant that forms dense mats or carpets close to the ground. This creeping perennial typically stays under 4 inches tall but can spread outward to create patches several feet wide. Its thick, fleshy leaves store water like tiny green cushions, and in late spring to early summer, it produces clusters of small yellow star-shaped flowers. **Note: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so identification details should be considered preliminary.**

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, thick, succulent leaves that feel plump and squishy when gently squeezed, arranged in opposite pairs or whorls of three along creeping stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow star-shaped flowers with 5 pointed petals, clustered together in small groups at stem tips, blooming in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with trailing stems that root at joints where they touch soil

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Reddish or purplish creeping stems that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, often rooting at nodes

habitat: **Uncertain due to limited New England data.** Based on its nature as a stonecrop, likely found in rocky areas, stone walls, or well-drained sandy soils. May occur in disturbed areas, gardens, or as an escape from cultivation in urban and suburban settings.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges and flower buds begin forming. The succulent leaves become most plump and vibrant green during spring moisture.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with bright yellow star-shaped blooms. Leaves may take on reddish tinges in hot, dry conditions.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants prepare for dormancy. Leaves often develop stronger red or purple coloration in cooler weather.
seasonality.winter: Plants remain low and dormant, though the succulent leaves may persist in milder conditions, often taking on deep red or purple winter colors.

funFact: Stonecrops can actually survive being completely dried out for weeks - their leaves will shrivel like raisins, but give them a good rain and they'll plump back up to life within hours, earning them the nickname 'resurrection plants' among gardeners.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spreading stonecrops, especially Stringy Stonecrop which also has yellow flowers. Look for Makino's stonecrop's more compact growth habit and the specific arrangement of its plump leaves in opposite pairs or groups of three.
contextualKnowledge: This species is primarily known as a garden plant in North America and is extremely rare in wild New England settings. Most stonecrop identifications in the region will likely be other more common species in the genus.
compareHints: Makino's stonecrop differs from Stringy Stonecrop by its more compact, less trailing growth habit and smaller stature. Unlike Biting Stonecrop, it lacks the sharp, peppery taste and has a more mat-forming growth pattern. Its yellow flowers distinguish it from White Stonecrop, while its creeping habit separates it from the more upright Woodland Stonecrop.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike biting stonecrop which has tiny needle-like leaves that taste peppery, stringy stonecrop has larger, flatter leaves in groups of three that are essentially tasteless.
Among New England stonecrops, biting stonecrop has the smallest, most tightly overlapping leaves and the most intense golden-yellow flowers.
Among New England's stonecrops, white stonecrop stands out for its pure white flowers and cylindrical leaves that look like tiny green hot dogs.
Tasteless stonecrop's six-spiral leaf arrangement sets it apart from most other stonecrops in New England.
Woodland stonecrop stands out from its stonecrop relatives by its preference for shade and its unique four-petaled white flowers – most other Sedum species have five yellow petals and love full sun.
Among New England's stonecrops, Spanish stonecrop is distinguished by its particularly dense, mat-forming growth and tendency toward reddish stem coloration.

Mexican Stonecrop stands out from other New England stonecrops by its bright yellow-green 'lemon coral' coloration, while Stringy Stonecrop is more blue-green and Biting Stonecrop has shorter, more tightly packed triangular leaves.

Unlike the common yellow-flowered biting stonecrop or the shade-loving woodland stonecrop with its distinctive three-leaf clusters, cliff stonecrop has pure white flowers and distinctly blue-green (glaucous) leaves.
Unlike the yellow-flowered biting stonecrop with its pointed, cone-shaped leaves, thick-leaved stonecrop has white or pink flowers and much plumper, rounder leaves.
